technique: Clay-Free Quartz Dough Preparation, POP Molding, and Surface Finishing
source_title: Blue Pottery of Jaipur — Tools, Raw Materials, and Making Process
source_organization: D'source (IDC School of Design, IIT Bombay & NID Digital Learning Initiative)
supported_facts: Jaipur Blue Pottery is crafted entirely without using ordinary potter's clay (mitti).
The dough is prepared from finely ground quartz stone powder, powdered glass (kaanch), Multani Mitti (Fuller's earth), Katira Gond (natural gum), Saaji (soda bicarbonate), and water.
Raw materials are ground in a chakki (grinder) and filtered through an iron sieve (jaali) before kneading with water.
Because the quartz dough lacks clay plasticity, forms are pressed into Plaster of Paris (POP) molds (saancha) rather than free-thrown into large vessels on a potter's wheel.
Dried molded items are trimmed with blades, rubbed on a base stone, and smoothed with sandpaper (regmaal) before coating.
steps: Crush and grind quartz stone, glass (kaanch), Multani Mitti, Katira Gond, and Saaji into fine powders and sieve through an iron mesh (jaali).
Mix the dry ingredients with water and knead thoroughly into a non-sticky quartz dough without any ordinary potter's clay.
Flatten and press the rested dough into Plaster of Paris (POP) molds, joining multi-part forms with dough slurry.
Dry the molded pieces, trim excess edges, rub on a base stone, and smooth the surface with sandpaper (regmaal).

technique: Cobalt & Copper Oxide Painting, Glazing, and Low-Temperature Kiln Firing
source_title: Blue Pottery of Jaipur — Art and Craft Documentation
source_organization: Department of Industries & Commerce, Government of Rajasthan (Handmade in Rajasthan)
supported_facts: Blue Pottery of Jaipur has Turko-Persian origins and was patronized in Jaipur under Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II.
Because the composition contains no ordinary clay, the pottery does not develop typical clay-shrinkage cracks.
The signature dark blue and azure colors are obtained from cobalt oxide, while turquoise and green tones are obtained from copper oxide.
Traditional floral, bird, and geometric motifs are hand-painted with fine brushes over a white ground coat (astar).
Glazed pieces undergo a single low-temperature firing in a kiln (bhatti), creating a vitrified, semi-transparent finish suited for vases, surahis, tiles, plates, and bowls.
steps: Apply an even white quartz-and-glass ground slip (astar) over the smoothed dry vessel and allow it to dry.
Outline and fill floral, bird, and geometric motifs by hand using fine brushes and metallic oxide pigments (cobalt oxide for blue, copper oxide for turquoise/green).
Coat the painted vessel with a transparent glass-based glaze.
Fire the glazed pieces in a single low-temperature kiln (bhatti) firing until the glass vitrifies.

technique: Tapestry Weft Interlocking, Reversible Construction, and Bangadi Mor Motif
source_title: Paithani Saree: Woven Histories of Maharashtra
source_organization: Sahapedia (Open Online Resource on the Arts and Cultures of India)
supported_facts: Paithani weaving originated in ancient Paithan (Pratishthana) under the Satavahanas and later established its primary handloom center in Yeola (Nashik district, Maharashtra).
Paithani sarees are woven using a handloom tapestry weft-interlocking technique where colored silk and zari weft threads are interlocked manually.
Because of tapestry interlocking, there are no loose floating threads on the reverse side, making the saree reversible with a nearly identical pattern on both front and back.
The iconic Bangadi Mor motif features a bangle (bangdi) enclosing a lotus flower surrounded by four dancing peacocks (mor).
Other documented traditional motifs include Munia (parrot) on borders, Asawali (flowering vine/creeper), and lotus designs inspired by the Ajanta Caves.
steps: Stretch the dyed mulberry silk warp (tana) across the handloom.
Weave the figured pallu and motifs using the tapestry technique, manually interlocking each colored silk and zari weft thread.
Ensure every weft interlock is tucked cleanly so no loose floating threads appear on the reverse side of the saree.
Weave traditional motifs such as Bangadi Mor (four peacocks inside a bangle ring), Munia (parrot), and Asawali (flowering vines).
materials: Mulberry silk warp and weft threads
Gold and silver metallic zari threads

technique: Mulberry Silk Degumming, Kadiyal Interlocking Border, and Zari Pallu Weaving
source_organization: All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association (AIACA) — Craftmark
supported_facts: Authentic handloom Paithani weaving uses pure mulberry silk for warp (tana) and weft (bana) along with fine metallic zari threads for borders and pallu.
Raw silk yarn is degummed/washed in warm alkaline water, dyed in fast colors, and wound onto reels and small bamboo spindles/bobbins (tilli) prior to loom warping.
In the Kadiyal interlocking border technique, shuttles (dhote) interlock the contrasting border warp and body weft threads along the selvedge without extra sewing.
steps: Degum and wash raw mulberry silk bundles in warm alkaline solution, then dye the yarn in vibrant fast colors.
Reel the dyed silk yarn and set up the warp (tana) on a traditional pit loom or frame handloom.
Use shuttles (dhote) for the Kadiyal border technique to interlock the border threads with the main body weft.
Interlace metallic zari and colored silk threads with small bamboo spindles (tilli) to form the dense zari pallu.
